claim_verdicts.evidence: Mirror collections.md: "A List<T> stores elements in order and can grow or shrink as your program runs." and "A sequence stores elements in order so you can reach them by position."; index is defined as "its zero-based position". commonly-used-collection-types.md l.61: "All collections use zero-based indexes except Array, which allows arrays that are not zero-based." Ran on SDK 10.0.300: `new List<int> { 2, 3, 2 }` printed `list count 3 l[0]=2 l[2]=2`.
claim_verdicts.source: refs/dotnet-docs/docs/csharp/fundamentals/statements/collections.md (Choose a collection shape; Grow and shrink a sequence with List<T>); .../standard/collections/commonly-used-collection-types.md l.61; local run (dotnet 10.0.300)

claim_verdicts.evidence: Ran on SDK 10.0.300: `new List<int> { 2, 3, 2 }` printed `list count 3 l[0]=2 l[2]=2` — both copies of 2 survived. Contrast is documented for the set only: hashtable-and-dictionary-collection-types.md: "The generic HashSet<T> class is an unordered collection for containing unique elements." Nothing in the List<T> documentation imposes a uniqueness constraint; Add is described as "append an element".

List<T>.Contains Remarks (page moniker net-10.0, default): "This method performs a linear search; therefore, this method is an O(n) operation, where n is Count." Measured on SDK 10.0.300 with a type that counts Equals calls: over a 10,000-element List, `list.Contains(new Box(9999))` produced `equalsCalls=10000`; the same query on a HashSet produced `equalsCalls=1`. Access by position performs no element comparison at all.

Mirror collections.md: "A dictionary stores values that you reach by key instead of by position. Use Dictionary<TKey,TValue> when each element has a lookup key, such as a name, ID, or code." and "A Dictionary<TKey,TValue> stores key/value pairs." One value per key confirmed by run on SDK 10.0.300: building a dictionary from two elements whose selector yields key 1 threw System.ArgumentException "An item with the same key has already been added. Key: 1".
claim_verdicts.source: refs/dotnet-docs/docs/csharp/fundamentals/statements/collections.md (Choose a collection shape; Associate a value by key); local run (dotnet 10.0.300)

claim_verdicts.evidence: Bucket-only search is documented: "the hash code is generated for that value, and the bucket associated with that hash code is searched"; "Dictionary<TKey,TValue> ... ha[s] the same functionality as the Hashtable class." Dictionary Remarks: "Retrieving a value by using its key is very fast, close to O(1), because the Dictionary<TKey,TValue> class is implemented as a hash table." But growth is documented as capacity, not bucket count: "As elements are added ..., the capacity is automatically increased as required by reallocating the internal array."
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: A hash-based lookup computes a hash code from the key and searches only the bucket associated with that hash code; the dictionary's capacity is automatically increased as elements are added, so retrieval stays close to O(1) as the collection grows. (Lesson wording "keeps more groups as it fills" is acceptable as plain language; the ledger should not assert bucket counts.)

claim_verdicts.evidence: Dictionary<TKey,TValue> Remarks: "The order in which the items are returned is undefined." No sentence on the page promises insertion order. Observed on SDK 10.0.300: a dictionary built with keys 1,2,3 enumerated as `1,2,3`; after `Remove(2)` and adding key 9 it enumerated as `1,9,3` — the new entry took the freed slot, so enumeration order is not insertion order.

Dictionary<TKey,TValue> Remarks: "As long as an object is used as a key in the Dictionary<TKey,TValue>, it must not change in any way that affects its hash value." Mechanism from hashtable-and-dictionary-collection-types.md: an object "is stored in the bucket that is associated with the hash code that matches the object's hash code", and a search generates the hash code and searches only that bucket — so a changed hash code sends the search elsewhere. (See the §4 issue: the lesson states the mechanism backwards.)

record.md: "For class types, two objects are equal if they refer to the same object in memory."; "For types with the record modifier ..., two objects are equal if they are of the same type and store the same values."; "To implement value equality, the compiler synthesizes several methods, including: An override of Object.Equals ... An override of Object.GetHashCode." Dictionary Remarks: "if you do not specify an implementation, the default generic equality comparer EqualityComparer<T>.Default is used." Run on 10.0.300: rebuilt record key found = True, rebuilt plain-class key found = False.

Ran on SDK 10.0.300: `byId[99]` on a dictionary built by ToDictionary threw System.Collections.Generic.KeyNotFoundException; `byId.TryGetValue(99, out _)` returned False without throwing. Dictionary Remarks: "The indexer throws an exception if the requested key is not in the dictionary." Mirror collections.md: "use Dictionary<TKey,TValue>.TryGetValue when the key might not exist" and "TryGetValue checks whether a key exists and gives you the value when it does."

Ran on SDK 10.0.300: `new List<Product> { new(1,"A",1), new(1,"D",4) }.ToDictionary(p => p.Id)` threw System.ArgumentException with message "An item with the same key has already been added. Key: 1" — the build aborts, which is what "refuses to finish" says. Single pass: the source is enumerated once and the key selector is applied per element; no second traversal is observable for the in-memory List<Product> the sample uses.

Ran the sample's own initializer on SDK 10.0.300: `new HashSet<int> { 2, 3, 2 }` printed `set count 2 add-again False` — the repeated 2 did not increase Count, and a later `Add(3)` on an element already present returned False, leaving the set unchanged. The real sample run prints "2 distinct ids, contains 3: True".
claim_verdicts.source: local run (dotnet 10.0.300); `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- collections-choice` at stage-0

claim_verdicts.evidence: Measured on SDK 10.0.300 with a key type that counts Equals calls: after inserting 10,000 elements into a HashSet, `set.Contains(new Box(9999))` returned True with `equalsCalls=1`. The same lookup over a 10,000-element List<Box> produced `equalsCalls=10000`. Mechanism documented: "the hash code is generated for that value, and the bucket associated with that hash code is searched" (Dictionary and HashSet share the hash-table shape).

Ran `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- collections-choice` on SDK 10.0.300 against the working tree at stage-0. Output verbatim: "1 Bàn phím cơ" / "2 Chuột không dây" / "3 Tai nghe" / "product 2 is Chuột không dây" / "2 distinct ids, contains 3: True" — exactly the lesson's expected result. The name is registered at Program.cs l.18: ["collections-choice"] = Sync(CollectionsChoice.Run).

The decision rule is the documented one. collections.md: "Choose the collection that matches how your code uses the data. A sequence stores elements in order so you can reach them by position ... A dictionary stores values that you reach by key instead of by position. Use Dictionary<TKey,TValue> when each element has a lookup key"; "Use foreach when you want to read every element in order." The set branch follows from "The generic HashSet<T> class is an unordered collection for containing unique elements."

The mechanical half is verified (see claims 3 and 17). The frequency half — "a common accidental slowness in junior code" — has no source. I grepped refs/dotnet-docs for statements about how often developers write a linear search inside a loop and found none, and no page under learn.microsoft.com/dotnet makes a claim about what junior developers typically write. Kind is opinion, so this does not block; but the lesson states it flatly ("a slowness junior code meets over and over") — see the §4 opinion-as-fact issue.
claim_verdicts.source: refs/dotnet-docs (grep, no match); content/tracks/foundation/track.yaml l.731 is the scope contract, not evidence

claim_verdicts.evidence: Shape verified: List<T>.Contains Remarks, "This method performs a linear search; therefore, this method is an O(n) operation, where n is Count", applied once per element of the outer collection gives a product, not a sum. Measured: one Contains over 10,000 elements cost exactly 10,000 Equals calls on SDK 10.0.300. Arithmetic in §4: 20 × 50,000 = 1,000,000 while 50,000 + 20 = 50,020. Note that the product is the worst case, since a linear search stops at the first match — see the §4 issue.

Verified by execution on SDK 10.0.300: `list.Find(predicate)` over a 10,000-element list recorded the predicate visiting ids 0,1,2,3 in that order before returning the element with Id 3 — forward from the first element, one comparison per element. But the parenthetical is stale: quiz q5 option b now names `products.IndexOf`, and neither the lesson nor any quiz option mentions `Find`. The ledger entry describes an assertion the material no longer makes.

`git -C examples/don-hang show stage-0:samples/DonHang.Samples/Samples/Data/CollectionsChoice.cs` gives l.3 `public sealed record Product(int Id, string Name, int PriceVnd);` — id, name, price in that order. `git grep collections-choice stage-0` gives Program.cs l.18: ["collections-choice"] = Sync(CollectionsChoice.Run). The §5 block (lines 10-27) matches the tagged source character-for-character after whitespace normalisation; `tools/extract-code ... --tag stage-0 --lines 10-27` reproduces it.

issues.text: Unlisted claim, and false as stated. The rule is given for any key type, but a plain struct defines neither Equals nor GetHashCode and still works as a key: ValueType supplies value-based equality. record.md: "For struct types, two objects are equal if they are of the same type and store the same values." Executed on SDK 10.0.300: a dictionary keyed by a bare `struct Pt { int X, Y; }` found the entry with a freshly built key (True). Claim 8 covers only record vs class; the lesson generalises past it.
issues.quote: Unless its type defines equality and a hash code by value, every instance counts as its own key, so a key you rebuild cannot find the entry you added.
issues.fix: Bound the rule to reference types: "Unless a key that is a class defines equality and a hash code by value, every instance counts as its own key, so a key you rebuild cannot find the entry you added." Keep the next sentence (record vs plain class) unchanged, and leave claim 8 as the ledger entry — no new claim is then needed.

issues.text: Option b describes a call that does not compile. `List<T>.IndexOf` takes a `T`, not a predicate, and the scenario searches by an order line's id, so there is no `Product` to hand it. Compiled on SDK 10.0.300: `products.IndexOf(p => p.Id == 2)` fails with "error CS1660: Cannot convert lambda expression to type 'Product' because it is not a delegate type". The key ('a') is unaffected, but the distractor teaches an API use that is impossible, and its explanation asserts IndexOf would do the search.
issues.quote: Replace the hand-written `foreach` and `if` with a call to `products.IndexOf`, so one method does the searching.
issues.fix: Use a method that takes a predicate: change option b (EN and VI) to name `products.Find`, and change `IndexOf` back to `Find` in option b's explanation. Then add `Find` to the §4 sentence that already names `Contains` and `IndexOf`, so the quiz only uses methods the lesson gave; claim 18 already covers Find's linear forward search.

issues.text: The mechanism is stated backwards. A stored entry is never re-filed when its key mutates: it stays in the bucket it was put in, and it is the later lookup that computes the new hash code and searches a different bucket. The documentation only says the key "must not change in any way that affects its hash value"; nothing says the dictionary moves entries. As written a reader can conclude the dictionary refiles entries behind their back.
issues.quote: a key whose hash code moves is filed in the wrong group and cannot be found
issues.fix: Move the failure to the lookup: "And it must not change while stored: the entry stays in the group it was filed under, so a key whose hash code has moved sends the lookup to a different group and the entry cannot be found."

issues.text: A number stated as exact that is only an upper bound. A linear search returns at the first match, so twenty searches over fifty thousand products cost a million comparisons only when every product searched for is the last one (or absent); the expected cost for matches spread evenly is about half that. The figure is right as a bound and wrong as a count, and the lesson gives it as a count.
issues.quote: twenty order lines against fifty thousand products means a million comparisons, not fifty thousand and twenty
issues.fix: Make it a bound: "twenty order lines against fifty thousand products means up to a million comparisons, not fifty thousand and twenty." Update claim 17's text the same way ("costs up to the product of the two sizes rather than their sum").

issues.text: A frequency claim about other developers, stated flatly and backed by nothing. Claim 16 is marked kind opinion with needs_verification false, but the sentence in the lesson reads as a fact about the world. I found no documentation source that measures how often this pattern appears in junior code, and none can exist in the sources this review may use.
issues.quote: a slowness junior code meets over and over
issues.fix: Attribute or drop it: "— the slowness the teammate was asking about." Or condition it: "a slowness that shows up whenever a search by content sits inside a loop." Either removes the unsupported claim about who writes what.

issues.text: The statement judged false is empirically true for this sample. With no removals, .NET's Dictionary enumerates in insertion order: observed on SDK 10.0.300, keys 1,2,3 came back as 1,2,3 and only after Remove(2) plus an add did the order become 1,9,3. A reader who runs the code sees the report print in written order, so "prints" is true today; only the contract makes option c right. Option c's wording carries the distinction, so the key is answerable, but the stem does not.
issues.quote: A report that walks `byId` prints the products in the order they were written in `products`, because `byId` was built from that list in one pass.
issues.fix: Put the reliance into the stem: "A report that walks `byId` can be relied on to print the products in the order they were written in `products`, because `byId` was built from that list in one pass." Answer stays 'c'; the VI stem needs the same change ("có thể dựa vào việc ... sẽ in").

issues.text: The dictionary paragraph goes from "compares only inside the small group" to "a lookup barely costs more as it grows" in one step. I cannot reconstruct why having more groups keeps a lookup cheap; nothing says that adding groups is what keeps each group short, so I have to take the claim on faith. It is the whole reason to prefer a dictionary, so I would rather understand it than believe it.
issues.quote: It keeps more groups as it fills, so a lookup barely costs more as it grows.
issues.fix: Between "the small group that number names." and "It keeps more groups as it fills" add one sentence saying that as more values arrive it keeps more groups, so each group stays a few values long and one lookup still compares only those few.
